subject: Geography
sub_topic: Rossby waves and upper air circulation

concepts.name: Rossby Waves: Origin and Formation Mechanism
key_dimensions: Role of Earth's rotation and the Coriolis effect in wave generation
Conservation of potential vorticity as the driving principle
Differential heating between poles and equator as the energy source
Distinction between thermally-driven vs. orographically-driven Rossby waves

concepts.name: Planetary vs. Synoptic Scale Waves: Classification and Differences
key_dimensions: Wavenumber 1–6 classification and their geographic scales
Rossby waves (planetary) vs. shorter baroclinic eddies (synoptic)
Role of each in meridional heat and momentum transport
UPSC trap: conflating all upper-air waves as 'Rossby waves'

concepts.name: Westerlies and the Polar Vortex: Structural Relationship
key_dimensions: Formation of the polar vortex and its coupling with the stratosphere
Role of Rossby waves in maintaining and disrupting the polar vortex
Sudden Stratospheric Warming (SSW) events and vortex weakening
Contrast between strong (zonal) and weak (meridional) polar vortex states

concepts.name: Jet Streams: Types, Location, and Seasonal Shifts
key_dimensions: Polar front jet stream vs. subtropical jet stream — formation differences
Tropical Easterly Jet (TEJ) over Indian subcontinent in summer
Seasonal north-south migration and its linkage to Indian monsoon onset
UPSC trap: Western Disturbances are associated with subtropical westerly jet, not polar jet

concepts.name: Rossby Wave Propagation: Eastward vs. Westward Movement
key_dimensions: Why Rossby waves propagate westward relative to mean flow
Stationary Rossby waves — conditions when wave speed equals mean westerly flow
Phase velocity vs. group velocity distinction in wave energy transport
Implications of stationary waves for persistent weather anomalies

concepts.name: Rossby Wave Breaking and Atmospheric Blocking
key_dimensions: Mechanism of wave breaking and irreversible overturning of potential vorticity
Anticyclonic vs. cyclonic wave breaking patterns
Formation of blocking highs (Omega blocks, Rex blocks) from wave breaking
Link between blocking events and extreme weather: heatwaves, cold spells, floods

concepts.name: Index Cycle: Zonal vs. Meridional Flow Regimes
key_dimensions: High zonal index (strong westerlies, fewer wave undulations) vs. low zonal index (amplified Rossby waves)
Cyclical transition between high and low index — roughly 3–8 week periodicity
Consequences for mid-latitude weather variability and storm tracks
UPSC trap: low index does NOT mean weaker winds everywhere — regional intensification occurs

concepts.name: Upper Air Circulation and Surface Weather Linkage
key_dimensions: Upper-level divergence/convergence and its role in surface cyclogenesis/anticyclogenesis
Vorticity advection aloft driving surface low pressure development
Left-exit and right-entrance regions of jet streaks as preferred cyclogenesis zones
Connection between 500 hPa trough/ridge patterns and surface frontal systems

concepts.name: Western Disturbances: Rossby Wave Connection to Indian Climate
key_dimensions: Embedded troughs in mid-latitude westerly waves that travel eastward toward India
Role in winter precipitation over northwest India, Pakistan, and the Himalayas
Interaction with the subtropical westerly jet stream (not polar jet)
Contrast with monsoon depressions — origin, season, and moisture source

concepts.name: Indian Monsoon Onset and the Upper Air Circulation Shift
key_dimensions: Northward shift of the subtropical jet stream triggering monsoon onset
Role of Tibetan High (anticyclone) development in upper troposphere
Tropical Easterly Jet (TEJ) as an indicator of active monsoon
UPSC trap: TEJ flows eastward (east), while subtropical westerly jet flows westward (west) — direction confusion

concepts.name: Arctic Amplification and Weakening of Rossby Waves
key_dimensions: Differential warming — Arctic warming faster than tropics reduces equator-to-pole temperature gradient
Reduced temperature gradient → weaker westerlies → more amplified (wavy) Rossby waves
Link to increased frequency of persistent weather extremes in mid-latitudes
Debate: scientific consensus vs. contested hypotheses (Jennifer Francis hypothesis)

concepts.name: Quasi-Biennial Oscillation (QBO) and Its Influence on Upper Air Waves
key_dimensions: QBO as alternating easterly-westerly wind regimes in the stratosphere (~28 km) with ~28-month cycle
QBO modulates the propagation of Rossby waves into the stratosphere
QBO westerly phase: stronger polar vortex; QBO easterly phase: weaker polar vortex
Interaction with ENSO to influence global weather patterns

concepts.name: El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) Teleconnections via Rossby Waves
key_dimensions: How equatorial heating anomalies (ENSO) excite Rossby wave trains in mid-latitudes
Pacific-North America (PNA) pattern as a classic ENSO-forced Rossby wave teleconnection
ENSO's remote influence on Indian monsoon, African rainfall, and Australian drought via wave trains
UPSC trap: ENSO impacts mid-latitude weather NOT just through direct atmospheric heating but via wave dynamics

concepts.name: Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) and Intraseasonal Upper Air Variability
key_dimensions: MJO as an eastward-propagating convective anomaly with 30–60 day periodicity
MJO excites both Kelvin waves (eastward) and Rossby waves (westward) in tropics
MJO modulation of Indian monsoon active and break cycles
Contrast MJO (intraseasonal) with ENSO (interannual) and QBO (quasi-biennial) timescales

concepts.name: Orographic Forcing of Stationary Rossby Waves
key_dimensions: How major mountain ranges (Himalayas, Rockies, Andes) act as obstacles deflecting airflow into wave patterns
Stationary wave pattern: persistent ridges downstream and troughs upstream of major orography
Tibetan Plateau as the world's most significant orographic forcing agent in the Northern Hemisphere
Role of stationary waves in determining climatological rainfall patterns globally

concepts.name: Upper Tropospheric Anticyclones and Divergence Zones
key_dimensions: Tibetan High / South Asian High — formation by diabatic heating over the plateau
Upper tropospheric anticyclone driving divergence and maintaining monsoon circulation
Mediterranean High in upper levels contrasting with surface subtropical highs
UPSC trap: upper-level anticyclone → surface convergence and low pressure (NOT surface high)

concepts.name: Sudden Stratospheric Warming (SSW) Events
key_dimensions: Upward-propagating Rossby waves from troposphere disrupt stratospheric polar vortex
Temperature rise of 30–50°C in days in the polar stratosphere during major SSW
Downward coupling: SSW leads to cold air outbreaks and negative Arctic Oscillation (AO) at surface weeks later
Distinction between minor SSW (deceleration only) and major SSW (wind reversal)

concepts.name: Arctic Oscillation (AO) and North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO): Wave-Driven Variability
key_dimensions: AO as the dominant mode of extratropical Northern Hemisphere variability — reflects polar vortex strength
Positive AO: strong polar vortex, Rossby waves confined poleward → mild mid-latitudes
Negative AO: weak polar vortex, amplified Rossby waves → cold air intrusions into mid-latitudes
NAO as the regional Atlantic sector expression of AO — influence on European and Indian weather

concepts.name: Storm Tracks and Rossby Wave Packet Propagation
key_dimensions: Baroclinic instability zones along polar front as genesis regions for extratropical cyclones
Rossby wave packets guiding the movement of successive cyclones along storm tracks
North Atlantic and North Pacific storm tracks — seasonal variation and climate change shifts
Impact of storm track shifts on monsoon variability and Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD)

concepts.name: Thermal Wind Relationship and Upper Air Wind Speed
key_dimensions: Thermal wind as the vertical shear of geostrophic wind driven by horizontal temperature gradients
Why jet streams are strongest at the tropopause level — maximum temperature gradient at polar front
Implications of thermal wind for vertical wind shear and tropical cyclone intensity
UPSC trap: thermal wind is NOT an actual wind but a mathematical relationship representing wind shear
